This measure assumes a distribution of energy consumption rates and capacities that align with the current baseline EV stock, as set by the “EV Battery” input. This measure may potentially overpredict the energy demand if EV technology makes advancements in efficiency and capacity over a certain adoption period. This current snapshot of battery efficiency and capacity may also overpredict unmet driving hours compared to future EV technologies with higher efficiencies. Additionally, ResStock limits dwelling units to a single EV, which is reasonable for capturing aggregate trends but may underestimate peak charging power in households with multiple EVs. As EV adoption scales, capturing these dynamics will be increasingly important for accurately modeling demand spikes and infrastructure needs. The inclusion of multi-family households introduces a modeling simplification. While residents in these units may not have ownership of charging infrastructure or see its impact on their utility bills, this approach treats EV charging as a household load, consistent with other building types. 12 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies (NLR) at www.nlr.gov/publications. 5 Results This section provides an overview of results from the “EV Adoption With L2 Charging” measure package and the baseline scenario. The results are presented to illustrate the measure’s performance and ensure confidence in its implementation, not to reflect a realistic scenario on its own. The measure is designed to offer the users flexibility when combined with the baseline or other measures. As such, results presented here should be interpreted with caution. Although this section presents the energy and unmet driving hour impacts of the measure, the full set of outputs available in the dataset includes annual and time series charging energy, charging emissions, utility bills, and EV schedules. Section 5.1 shows the overall stock energy consumption, Section 5.2 displays the unmet driving hours, and Section 5.3 shows samples of time series data. 5.1 Annual Stock Energy Consumption Figure 4 presents the distributions of annual ResStock energy usage for the baseline and the measure at the national level. With broad adoption of EVs and L2 chargers (87.9% of the housing stock), the national site energy usage increases by 7.2%, which is entirely driven by increases in EV charging electricity demand. Figure 5 shows annual stock energy consumption by Building America climate zone. Stock energy consumption expectedly increases with the “EV Adoption With L2 Charging” measure package in all climate zones. While EV charging loads are influenced by outdoor temperatures, the effect is much smaller compared to heating, ventilation, and air conditioning (HVAC) loads. As a result, the measure’s percentage of change in total energy usage is mostly driven by the proportion of baseline HVAC energy usage, where milder climates will exhibit a higher percentage energy increase from EV adoption.
